transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Mostly I came in because I’m just… tired, I guess is the simplest way to say it, but it doesn’t feel like normal tired. I can sleep, and I’m still able to get through my work and do what I need to do, but it’s like I’m running on a low battery before the day has even really started.

I manage computer systems, so I’m used to juggling things and keeping my head in the game, and I can still do that, but lately—or maybe not even lately, it just feels like it’s been there—I notice I’m pushing myself through the day more than I think I should have to. It doesn’t really make sense to me, because it’s not like I’m staying up all night or anything. It’s more that I wake up and already feel worn down, like I’m starting from behind.
Do you find yourself enjoying things you normally like to do?

Yeah… I do, but not the way I used to. It’s hard to explain without making it sound more dramatic than it is, but for a long time now there’s been this sort of gray, flat feeling most days. Like the color’s been turned down on things.

I still do things I’ve always liked. I’ll go fishing sometimes, or I’ll go out and tend to the tomatoes, or if there’s a concert at church I might go. Those used to be things I’d look forward to a bit, you know, something that gave me a little lift. Now they can feel more like… well, like items on a checklist. I’ll think, okay, I should go fishing, that’s something I enjoy, or I should get out in the garden because it’s good to keep up with it. But when I’m doing it, it doesn’t really land the same. It’s not miserable exactly. It’s just kind of flat.
How long have you been feeling this way?

It’s been… I’d say about two years and four months, give or take. I can actually tie it pretty closely to when I got pulled back into full operational leadership at work. Before that, I don’t want to say everything was perfect, but I didn’t feel this same kind of long, steady grayness hanging over things.

Once I was back in that role, with everything on my shoulders again day to day, that’s when I noticed it settling in. And it didn’t really come and go in any clean way. It’s more like it became the background noise of my life, and after a while I stopped expecting it to lift on its own.
Do you still find pleasure in social interactions or has that also become flat for you?

It’s become flatter, yes. I wouldn’t say I get nothing out of being around people, but it doesn’t have the same feeling it used to. It’s similar to the other things I mentioned—fishing, the tomatoes, going to a church concert—things I know I used to look forward to more. Now I’ll still show up, I’ll still talk, I’ll still do what you’re supposed to do socially, but inside it can feel kind of gray, like I’m going through the motions.

It’s not that I dislike people or anything like that. I’m not sitting there thinking, “I wish I hadn’t come.” It’s more that the pleasure part is muted. Like I can recognize, logically, “This is a nice conversation,” or “It’s good to see these folks,” but it doesn’t really lift me much. It ends up feeling a bit like another item on the day’s list, instead of something that restores me.
Have you ever had thoughts of not wanting to be alive or wishing you could just disappear?

I… I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly. I wouldn’t say I’ve had some clear thought like, “I want to die,” if that’s what you mean. It’s more that sometimes I get worn down and I think it would be nice to not have to deal with anything for a while, or to sort of step out of everything. But I don’t know that I’d call that not wanting to be alive.

The “disappear” part is closer, maybe, but even that sounds stronger than I mean it. It’s more like wanting to be left alone, wanting the phone to stop, wanting nobody to need anything from me. Not vanish forever. Just… not have to carry everything for a bit.

So, no, I don’t think I’ve had those thoughts in a serious way. But I do understand the feeling of wanting everything to go quiet.
Do you often feel anxious or on edge?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way, honestly. I mean, I get stressed, sure, and I can get tense when there’s a lot happening or people are waiting on me for answers. But “anxious or on edge” sounds like something more constant or jumpy, and I don’t know that I’ve noticed that as the main thing.

It’s more like I’m tired of having to keep track of everything, if that makes sense. Sometimes I’m bracing for the next call or the next problem, but I don’t know if that’s anxiety exactly or just… being worn down. I wouldn’t say I’m panicky or sitting there trembling or anything like that.

So, maybe some stress, yes. But often anxious or on edge? I’m not sure. I don’t think that’s the best description of it.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past couple of years?

Yeah… I think so, though I haven’t been tracking it carefully on a scale or anything. It’s more something I noticed after my wife pointed it out. She said my pants were looking looser, and I realized she was probably right. I’m not trying to lose weight, so it’s not like I’ve been dieting or exercising more on purpose.

My appetite’s just been kind of off, more days than not. I’ll get busy and work straight through lunch without really noticing I haven’t eaten, and then by dinner I’ll sit down and sort of pick at the food. It’s not that the food tastes bad exactly, I just don’t feel that pull to eat like I used to. Then later I might realize, “Oh, I didn’t really have much today.”

So I wouldn’t say I’ve had some dramatic weight drop that I can put a number on, but yes, there’s been enough change that my clothes fit differently, and other people have noticed it.
Have you had thoughts about death recurring in your mind?

Not really, no. I mean… I suppose everybody thinks about death now and then, especially as you get older and you hear about someone from your past getting sick or passing away. So it’s not like the word never crosses my mind.

But if you mean it keeps coming back on its own, or I’m sitting there dwelling on it, turning it over and over, then no, I don’t think so. I haven’t noticed that as a recurring thing. It’s not something I feel preoccupied with or pulled toward. Usually if it comes up, it’s because something reminded me of it, not because my mind is stuck there.
Do you find yourself moving or reacting more slowly than you used to?

I’m not sure, honestly. I haven’t really noticed myself moving slowly in the way I think you mean, like shuffling around or taking forever to get up from a chair. Nobody at home has said, “Why are you moving so slowly?” or anything like that.

At work, sometimes I may take longer to get through things, but that feels more like I’m getting bogged down or having to reread something, not that my body is physically slowed down. And I’m 63, so I’m not exactly rushing around like I did when I was younger, but I don’t know that there’s been some clear change where I’m reacting much slower than before.

So… I guess I’d say no, not that I’ve noticed. If it’s happening, it’s not obvious to me.
Do you often feel guilty about things or blame yourself for problems?

I don’t know that I’d call it guilt exactly. I mean, I can second-guess myself, sure. If something doesn’t go well, especially at work or with something I was supposed to handle at home, I’ll replay it in my head and think, “Well, maybe I should’ve done that differently.” But I’m not walking around feeling like everything is my fault, if that’s what you mean.

Blaming myself… sometimes I probably take more responsibility than I need to, but it’s not like I’m consumed by guilt or thinking I’m a terrible person. It’s more ordinary regret or frustration, I guess. Like, “I could’ve handled that better,” and then I move on, or try to. So no, not often in a big way.
Are your feelings of tiredness and flatness present for most of the day, or do they come and go?

Most of the day, I’d say. It’s not like I wake up feeling wonderful and then suddenly it hits at three o’clock. It’s more like this background color to the day, if that makes sense — kind of gray and flat. It’s been that way for a long time now, most days.

I can still do things. I mean, I’ll go through the motions. I’ll go fishing if I planned to, or I’ll tend the tomatoes, or go to a church concert if that’s on the calendar. But a lot of the time those things feel more like items on a checklist than things I’m really looking forward to or getting much out of. Sometimes there are little moments where it lifts a bit, but generally it’s just… there. Not dramatic, just steady.
Are there any activities that you still find give you a sense of pleasure or enjoyment?

I wish I could say yes in a straightforward way, but… not really, at least not the way I used to.

I still do some of the same things. I’ll go fishing, for example, and I used to really look forward to that — getting the gear together, being out there, even if I didn’t catch much. And I still go sometimes, but it’s more like, “Well, this is what I said I was going to do,” or “It’s good to get out of the house.” Same with tending the tomatoes. I’ll water them, check on them, do what needs doing, and I guess there’s some satisfaction in keeping them alive and seeing them grow, but it doesn’t really land as pleasure the way it used to.

Church concerts are similar. I can sit there and know it’s good music, and I’m glad people put the effort in, but inside I often feel kind of flat. Like I’m present, but not fully taking it in. Most days there’s just this gray feeling over things, and activities that used to feel enjoyable now feel more like items on a checklist. I can still do them, and sometimes there might be a small moment where I think, “That was nice,” but it’s pretty muted.
Have you had any periods, even brief ones, where you felt significantly better over the past two years?

Not really, no. I mean, there have been a day here or there where I’ve been a little more functional, or something went smoothly and I thought, “Okay, that wasn’t so bad,” but I wouldn’t say I’ve had a stretch where I felt significantly better.

This all sort of started when I got pulled back into full operational leadership at work, which was… let me think… about two years and four months ago now. And since then it’s been pretty steady. There hasn’t been some clear month or even a couple weeks where I felt like I was back to my old self. Maybe brief little lifts, but nothing I’d call a real improvement.
Have you experienced a period of at least two weeks where you felt depressed or lost interest in most activities?

Yes, I think so. More than two weeks, really. It’s been… a long time now that most days have had this gray, flat feeling to them.

It’s not always like I’m crying or completely unable to function or anything like that. I still do things — I’ll go fishing, I’ll tend the tomatoes, I’ll show up for a church concert if that’s what’s going on — but it’s like the enjoyment got turned way down. Those things used to be something I’d look forward to, and now they feel more like things I’m checking off a list because I know I should keep doing them.

So yes, I’d say there have definitely been periods of at least two weeks where I felt depressed or just didn’t really have much interest or pleasure in most things. Honestly, it’s been more steady than brief.
Are there any days where you wake up feeling like your normal self, without this gray, flat feeling?

Not really, no. I mean… I suppose there are mornings where it’s not quite as heavy right away, where I can get up and make coffee and start moving without thinking about it too much. But I wouldn’t say I wake up and feel like my normal self, not in the way I remember feeling before.

Most days there’s still that gray, flat sort of feeling there, even if it’s quieter some mornings than others. It’s like it’s already in the room when I wake up. And then the day becomes doing the things I’m supposed to do — go fishing if I planned to, water the tomatoes, show up at a church concert — and I can recognize those are good things, but they don’t feel the same. They’re more like tasks I’m completing than things I’m really enjoying.

So… no, I don’t really have days where I wake up and think, “Oh, there I am, I’m back to normal.” Maybe little moments that are less bad, but not a whole day without that flatness.

Have you had at least five of the following symptoms nearly every day for the past two weeks: depressed mood, markedly diminished interest or pleasure in activities, significant weight loss or gain, insomnia or hypersomnia, psychomotor agitation or retardation, fatigue or loss of energy, feelings of worthlessness or guilt, diminished ability to think or concentrate, or recurrent thoughts of death?

Well, the ones I can speak to for sure are the depressed mood and the loss of interest or pleasure. That’s been there nearly every day, yes.

For a long time now there’s just been this gray, flat feeling most days. It’s not always dramatic, like I’m visibly falling apart or anything, but it’s there in the background. Even things I used to genuinely look forward to — fishing, working with the tomatoes, going to a church concert — they don’t land the same way anymore. I still do them, but it feels more like I’m moving through a checklist than actually enjoying them.

So if you’re asking whether those two have been present over the past couple of weeks, yes, definitely. The rest of that list… I’m not sure I’d want to say yes to five of them without thinking carefully, but the mood and the lack of enjoyment are very much there.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight over the past two years?

I haven’t been tracking it closely on a scale, so I don’t know the exact number, but… yes, I think I probably have lost some weight over that time. Not because I was trying to.

My appetite’s just been off more days than not. I’ll get into work or get wrapped up in something and realize I worked straight through lunch without even really noticing I was hungry. Then at dinner I’ll sit down with my wife and kind of pick at what’s there instead of eating like I used to. It’s not every single meal, but it’s happened enough that she’s commented on it.

She’s also pointed out that my pants are fitting looser, and I’ve noticed that too. I kept thinking maybe they were just stretched out or something, but it’s probably more than that. So I wouldn’t want to claim some exact big number, but there has been weight loss, and it wasn’t intentional.
Would you say your weight loss over the past two years has been significant, such as more than 5% of your body weight?

I don’t know if I can honestly put a percentage on it. I haven’t been weighing myself regularly, so I’d be guessing if I said, “Yes, it’s definitely more than 5%.” It may be, but I can’t say that with confidence.

What I can say is that my appetite has been off more days than not. I’ll work right through lunch without really noticing, and then by dinner I’m sitting there with my wife and sort of picking at the food instead of eating a normal meal. And it’s not because I’m trying to lose weight or watching what I eat.

My wife has noticed my pants are fitting looser, and I’ve noticed that too. So there has been some weight loss, I think. Whether it crosses that 5% line, I’m just not sure.
Has this gray, flat feeling you've described lasted for at least two years continuously?

Yes… yes, I’d say it has. It started around the time I got pulled back into full operational leadership at work, which was about two years and four months ago now.

I remember it because it felt like a pretty clear dividing line. Before that, I wouldn’t say I was carefree or anything, but I still had more moments where things felt normal. Then once I was back in that role, day after day, it was like this grayness settled in and just never really lifted. Some days are a little lighter than others, I guess, but I don’t think there’s been any real stretch where I felt like myself again.

So if you mean continuously as in, “Has it basically been there most of the time since then?” — yes. About two years and four months.
Has this gray, flat feeling you've described been present for most of every day over the past two years?

Yes… I think that’s fair to say. It’s not like every single minute of every single day I’m sitting there thinking, “I feel gray,” but most days, and for a lot of the day, it’s there in the background.

It’s this flat feeling, like things don’t have the same color to them. I still do things — I’ll go fishing, I’ll tend to the tomatoes, I’ll go to a church concert if it’s on the calendar — but a lot of the time it feels more like I’m checking something off than actually looking forward to it or enjoying it the way I used to.

Sometimes I can get distracted for a bit, especially if there’s something that needs doing, but when things quiet down, that same dull, gray feeling is just there again. So yes, I’d say it’s been present most days, and most of the day, for a long time now.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about loss of pleasure or enjoyment in activities, which is directly reflected in the depressed mood profile manifestation where previously enjoyable activities feel like checklist items rather than enjoyable.

patient.answer:
I wish I could say yes in a straightforward way, but… not really, at least not the way I used to.

I still do some of the same things. I’ll go fishing, for example, and I used to really look forward to that — getting the gear together, being out there, even if I didn’t catch much. And I still go sometimes, but it’s more like, “Well, this is what I said I was going to do,” or “It’s good to get out of the house.” Same with tending the tomatoes. I’ll water them, check on them, do what needs doing, and I guess there’s some satisfaction in keeping them alive and seeing them grow, but it doesn’t really land as pleasure the way it used to.

Church concerts are similar. I can sit there and know it’s good music, and I’m glad people put the effort in, but inside I often feel kind of flat. Like I’m present, but not fully taking it in. Most days there’s just this gray feeling over things, and activities that used to feel enjoyable now feel more like items on a checklist. I can still do them, and sometimes there might be a small moment where I think, “That was nice,” but it’s pretty muted.

patient.answer:
Not really, no. I mean, there have been a day here or there where I’ve been a little more functional, or something went smoothly and I thought, “Okay, that wasn’t so bad,” but I wouldn’t say I’ve had a stretch where I felt significantly better.

This all sort of started when I got pulled back into full operational leadership at work, which was… let me think… about two years and four months ago now. And since then it’s been pretty steady. There hasn’t been some clear month or even a couple weeks where I felt like I was back to my old self. Maybe brief little lifts, but nothing I’d call a real improvement.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the criteria for a depressive episode
doctor.question: Have you experienced a period of at least two weeks where you felt depressed or lost interest in most activities?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: For a long time now there’s been this gray, flat feeling most days, where even things I used to look forward to like fishing, tending the tomatoes, or a church concert feel like items on a checklist instead of something I enjoy.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about having a sustained period of depressed mood or loss of interest in activities, which is most directly covered by Depressed_Mood.

patient.answer:
Yes, I think so. More than two weeks, really. It’s been… a long time now that most days have had this gray, flat feeling to them.

It’s not always like I’m crying or completely unable to function or anything like that. I still do things — I’ll go fishing, I’ll tend the tomatoes, I’ll show up for a church concert if that’s what’s going on — but it’s like the enjoyment got turned way down. Those things used to be something I’d look forward to, and now they feel more like things I’m checking off a list because I know I should keep doing them.

So yes, I’d say there have definitely been periods of at least two weeks where I felt depressed or just didn’t really have much interest or pleasure in most things. Honestly, it’s been more steady than brief.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's depressive symptoms are persistent or intermittent
doctor.question: Are there any days where you wake up feeling like your normal self, without this gray, flat feeling?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: For a long time now there’s been this gray, flat feeling most days, where even things I used to look forward to like fishing, tending the tomatoes, or a church concert feel like items on a checklist instead of something I enjoy.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the gray, flat depressed mood is present on waking or if there are days without it, which directly relates to persistent depressed mood.

patient.answer:
Not really, no. I mean… I suppose there are mornings where it’s not quite as heavy right away, where I can get up and make coffee and start moving without thinking about it too much. But I wouldn’t say I wake up and feel like my normal self, not in the way I remember feeling before.

Most days there’s still that gray, flat sort of feeling there, even if it’s quieter some mornings than others. It’s like it’s already in the room when I wake up. And then the day becomes doing the things I’m supposed to do — go fishing if I planned to, water the tomatoes, show up at a church concert — and I can recognize those are good things, but they don’t feel the same. They’re more like tasks I’m completing than things I’m really enjoying.

So… no, I don’t really have days where I wake up and think, “Oh, there I am, I’m back to normal.” Maybe little moments that are less bad, but not a whole day without that flatness.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the criteria for a major depressive episode
doctor.question: Have you had at least five of the following symptoms nearly every day for the past two weeks: depressed mood, markedly diminished interest or pleasure in activities, significant weight loss or gain, insomnia or hypersomnia, psychomotor agitation or retardation, fatigue or loss of energy, feelings of worthlessness or guilt, diminished ability to think or concentrate, or recurrent thoughts of death?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood

patient.answer:
Well, the ones I can speak to for sure are the depressed mood and the loss of interest or pleasure. That’s been there nearly every day, yes.

For a long time now there’s just been this gray, flat feeling most days. It’s not always dramatic, like I’m visibly falling apart or anything, but it’s there in the background. Even things I used to genuinely look forward to — fishing, working with the tomatoes, going to a church concert — they don’t land the same way anymore. I still do them, but it feels more like I’m moving through a checklist than actually enjoying them.

So if you’re asking whether those two have been present over the past couple of weeks, yes, definitely. The rest of that list… I’m not sure I’d want to say yes to five of them without thinking carefully, but the mood and the lack of enjoyment are very much there.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of significant weight loss
doctor.question: Have you lost a significant amount of weight over the past two years?

patient.answer:
I haven’t been tracking it closely on a scale, so I don’t know the exact number, but… yes, I think I probably have lost some weight over that time. Not because I was trying to.

My appetite’s just been off more days than not. I’ll get into work or get wrapped up in something and realize I worked straight through lunch without even really noticing I was hungry. Then at dinner I’ll sit down with my wife and kind of pick at what’s there instead of eating like I used to. It’s not every single meal, but it’s happened enough that she’s commented on it.

She’s also pointed out that my pants are fitting looser, and I’ve noticed that too. I kept thinking maybe they were just stretched out or something, but it’s probably more than that. So I wouldn’t want to claim some exact big number, but there has been weight loss, and it wasn’t intentional.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of significant weight loss
doctor.question: Would you say your weight loss over the past two years has been significant, such as more than 5% of your body weight?

target_item.name: Weight_Appetite_Change
target_item.manifestation: My appetite has been off more days than not, so I’ll work through lunch without noticing and then pick at dinner, and my wife has pointed out my pants are looser even though I’m not trying to lose weight.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically whether the patient's weight loss over the past two years has been significant, including whether it exceeds 5% of body weight.

patient.answer:
I don’t know if I can honestly put a percentage on it. I haven’t been weighing myself regularly, so I’d be guessing if I said, “Yes, it’s definitely more than 5%.” It may be, but I can’t say that with confidence.

What I can say is that my appetite has been off more days than not. I’ll work right through lunch without really noticing, and then by dinner I’m sitting there with my wife and sort of picking at the food instead of eating a normal meal. And it’s not because I’m trying to lose weight or watching what I eat.

My wife has noticed my pants are fitting looser, and I’ve noticed that too. So there has been some weight loss, I think. Whether it crosses that 5% line, I’m just not sure.

target_item.name: Duration

patient.answer:
Yes… yes, I’d say it has. It started around the time I got pulled back into full operational leadership at work, which was about two years and four months ago now.

I remember it because it felt like a pretty clear dividing line. Before that, I wouldn’t say I was carefree or anything, but I still had more moments where things felt normal. Then once I was back in that role, day after day, it was like this grayness settled in and just never really lifted. Some days are a little lighter than others, I guess, but I don’t think there’s been any real stretch where I felt like myself again.

So if you mean continuously as in, “Has it basically been there most of the time since then?” — yes. About two years and four months.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms meet the duration criteria for a persistent depressive disorder
doctor.question: Has this gray, flat feeling you've described been present for most of every day over the past two years?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: For a long time now there’s been this gray, flat feeling most days, where even things I used to look forward to like fishing, tending the tomatoes, or a church concert feel like items on a checklist instead of something I enjoy.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about the persistence and daily presence of the gray, flat mood, which directly corresponds to depressed mood.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think that’s fair to say. It’s not like every single minute of every single day I’m sitting there thinking, “I feel gray,” but most days, and for a lot of the day, it’s there in the background.

It’s this flat feeling, like things don’t have the same color to them. I still do things — I’ll go fishing, I’ll tend to the tomatoes, I’ll go to a church concert if it’s on the calendar — but a lot of the time it feels more like I’m checking something off than actually looking forward to it or enjoying it the way I used to.

Sometimes I can get distracted for a bit, especially if there’s something that needs doing, but when things quiet down, that same dull, gray feeling is just there again. So yes, I’d say it’s been present most days, and most of the day, for a long time now.
